data.title: C-frame or H-frame: choosing the right press for your die
data.excerpt: Frame geometry decides how a press handles off-centre loads. Here is how to choose between the two.
data.cover_alt: C-frame or H-frame: choosing the right press for your die

children.text: The frame is the part of a press you cannot replace later, so it is worth getting right. A C-frame press opens on the left, which gives a clear view of the working area and easy access to the die — the usual choice for general stamping. An H-frame opens on both sides, which is what you want for wide or multi-column tooling and for loading from both ends. Off-centre loads punish a narrow frame, so match the tonnage rating to the real load rather than the peak figure a supplier quotes. If you are ever unsure, send us the die dimensions and the thinnest material you intend to form, and we will size it with you.

data.title: What actually keeps a power press running year after year
data.excerpt: A short list of the things that decide whether a press is still accurate in its tenth year.
data.cover_alt: What actually keeps a power press running year after year

children.text: Presses do not fail suddenly. They drift. The most common causes are a clutch that has lost its adjustment, a slide running out of parallel because the gibs have worn, and lubrication that was scheduled but never carried out. A weekly fifteen-minute check — gib lubrication, clutch-brake response, and the noise each slide makes on the downstroke — catches nearly all of it. Keep a log. When the same sound changes, you have a problem weeks before the press stops. The machines we build are designed so that these checks are reachable without stripping the slide, and we ship a maintenance schedule with every machine we hand over.

data.title: How to choose press tonnage without over-buying
data.excerpt: Tonnage is the number people overthink. It is mostly arithmetic once you have the numbers.
data.cover_alt: How to choose press tonnage without over-buying
How to choose press tonnage without over-buying

children.text: Work out the force your job actually needs — the perimeter of the cut times the material thickness times the shear strength, then divide by the efficiency of your press. That gives a working figure. Then choose the machine above it that sits closest to your normal load rather than the one above your absolute worst case, because a press that only ever sees a fraction of its rating never gets into its efficient band. Buying the larger machine "to be safe" costs you capital and floor space, and it is also slower. If your load varies a lot, tell us the range rather than a single number and we will recommend a machine that covers the bulk of it well.

data.title: Cross Shaft Power Presses
data.excerpt: Cross-shaft drive presses for steady, high-tonnage stamping.

children.text: Cross-shaft drive presses for steady, high-tonnage stamping. In a cross-shaft press the crankshaft runs across the machine, driven through gears from the flywheel, so each stroke draws on stored flywheel energy. That layout suits steady blanking and forming work where the load is heavy but the stroke rate is moderate.

data.title: H Frame Mechanical Power Press
data.excerpt: H-frame presses open on both sides for wide tooling and end-to-end loading.

children.text: H-frame presses open on both sides for wide tooling and end-to-end loading. The H frame leaves the working area clear from both ends, which matters for wide dies, multi-column tooling, and parts that load from one side and exit the other.

data.title: C Frame Mechanical Power Press
data.excerpt: Gap-frame presses with open access for general stamping and quick die changes.

children.text: Gap-frame presses with open access for general stamping and quick die changes. The C frame leaves the front of the working area completely open, so operators can see the die, feed strip or blanks by hand, and change tooling quickly.

data.title: Knuckle Joint Press
data.excerpt: Knuckle-action presses that peak in force at the bottom of a short, rigid stroke.

children.text: Knuckle-action presses that peak in force at the bottom of a short, rigid stroke. A knuckle mechanism multiplies force exactly where coining, embossing and sizing need it, then opens fast for part removal.
